title: SpaceX and Tesla Put the Cost of AI in Focus
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

SpaceX and Tesla’s earnings this week will test whether Elon Musk’s established businesses can support his increasingly expensive artificial intelligence ambitions. SpaceX reports Tuesday, followed by Tesla on Wednesday, as speculation builds about a potential merger. Neither company nor Musk has formally endorsed a deal.

For SpaceX, investors will watch whether Starlink’s growth and emerging AI revenue justify enormous investment. Analysts expect quarterly revenue of approximately $12.74 billion. The company spent $15.8 billion on AI capital investment in the previous quarter, illustrating the scale of its commitment.

Tesla faces a related challenge: translating vehicle sales into sufficient profits while financing robotaxis, humanoid robots and AI infrastructure. Analysts forecast revenue of about $27.88 billion and adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share, below 50 cents a year earlier. Despite stronger vehicle deliveries, substantial spending is expected to push quarterly free cash flow deeply negative.

Why it matters: These reports could help investors judge whether Musk’s vision rests on sustainable business economics. Revenue growth alone cannot establish that; the critical questions concern margins, cash generation and the eventual returns from today’s spending.

A merger would also raise questions beyond technological overlap. Combining businesses could make it easier to coordinate investment, but shareholders would need to examine valuation, ownership, voting control and how financial risks are distributed. Shared leadership does not automatically mean a transaction benefits both groups equally.

The wider significance is the discipline required to turn AI enthusiasm into durable earnings. Investors evaluating ambitious technology projects need evidence that customers will pay enough to cover infrastructure, operating costs and future expansion.

My assessment is that the most revealing signals will be management’s spending commitments and explanations of when investments should produce cash. Those details will show how much patience shareholders are being asked to supply, and on what financial terms.
